extracted.intended_audience: trial judges and litigators preparing or using model patent jury instructions
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent litigation that judges and attorneys can use and tailor for trials; covers claim construction, infringement (direct and indirect), invalidity burdens, damages, and related jury guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two Types of Damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages for patent infringement generally fall into two types: lost profits and reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See detailed sections on lost profits (including Panduit factors and various sub-issues) and reasonable royalty (including the hypothetical negotiation method and relevant factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits – "But-For" Test
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits damages are assessed under a 'but-for' causation test — what profits would the patent owner have made but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Panduit factors and subtopics (demand, acceptable non-infringing substitutes, market share, capacity, incremental profit approaches, price erosion, cost escalation, collateral sales, doubts resolved against infringer) for elements needed to support a lost-profits award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factors for Lost Profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Panduit four-factor test to establish entitlement to lost profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors enumerated: (1) demand for the patented product, (2) absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes, (3) the manufacturing and marketing capacity to exploit the demand, and (4) the amount of profit that would have been made (incremental income). Related issues: market share, capacity, price erosion, cost escalation, collateral sales; doubts resolved against infringer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty — Hypothetical Negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is often calculated using a hypothetical negotiation framework — what royalty would the parties have agreed to at the time infringement began.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider relevant factors (listed elsewhere in the Instructions), multiple patents, timing of the negotiation, availability of non-infringing substitutes, and post-trial adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful infringement (enhanced damages) is a distinct issue addressed after liability is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See sections on willfulness generally and issues such as absence of a legal opinion; willfulness analysis affects possible enhanced damages but requires separate instruction and factual findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents and What They Give (Background for Jury)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent gives the owner the right to exclude others from making, using, offering to sell, selling, or importing the patented invention in the United States; the specification should describe the invention and how to make and use it; claims define the invention's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide jurors with a glossary and technical background; explain prosecution history/file wrapper and prior art concepts (publicly available before the invention or more than one year before filing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of Validity and Burden for Invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is presumed valid; the accused infringer must overcome that presumption by clear and convincing evidence to establish invalidity (or unenforceability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing evidence is defined as highly probable and is a higher standard than preponderance of the evidence but lower than beyond a reasonable doubt. Jury must apply same claim construction for infringement and invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's Burden to Prove Infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent owner (plaintiff) must prove infringement by a preponderance of the evidence — more likely than not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plaintiff must show that the accused product or method meets each element of at least one asserted claim (literal infringement) or, if arguing equivalents, that equivalents exist for missing claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction — Judge's Role
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the court's job to determine the meaning of claim language; jurors must accept and use the judge's constructions in assessing infringement and invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the claims define the boundaries of the invention; written description and drawings themselves are not infringed. Use the same claim meaning for both infringement and invalidity determinations. Follow governing authorities (e.g., Phillips, Markman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction for Means-Plus-Function (35 U.S.C. § 112 ¶ 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function (or step-plus-function) clauses cover only the structure (or step) described in the specification that performs the function or an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court must identify the structure in the specification that performs the recited function and instruct the jury accordingly. Instruction 2.2 is recommended to avoid jury confusion where §112 ¶6 limitations are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement — Elements Present (Literal Infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is literally infringed only if the accused product/method includes each and every element or step recited in that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine literal infringement for each claim individually by comparing the accused product/method to the claim language using the court's claim constructions. The same accused feature may satisfy multiple claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the doctrine of equivalents, infringement may be found even if not every claim element is literally present, if an equivalent exists for each absent element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that equivalents exist for the missing elements so that the accused product/method contains the equivalent of each claim element not literally present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Infringement — Knowledge and Intent Immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of the patent and intent to infringe are immaterial to direct infringement liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defendant can directly infringe without knowing of the patent or believing in good faith that its conduct does not infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Infringement (Divided Performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where separate entities perform different steps of a claimed method, liability can attach if steps performed by another were performed on behalf of the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the defendant exercised control or direction over the other party when it performed such steps; a contractual requirement for performance by the other party can indicate authority and liability. Note Federal Circuit en banc developments may affect this area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducing Infringement — Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove inducement (35 U.S.C. §271(b)) the plaintiff must establish by a preponderance that: (1) the defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with intent to cause acts by another that would constitute direct infringement; (2) the defendant knew of the patent or was willfully blind to its existence; (3) the defendant knew or should have known that its actions would result in infringement of at least one claim; and (4) another actually directly infringed at least one claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Willful blindness requires a subjective belief that there was a high probability that a patent existed and deliberate actions to avoid learning of it. Inducement requires an underlying direct infringement — without any direct infringement, inducement cannot be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory Infringement — Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish contributory infringement (35 U.S.C. §271(c)), the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that: (1) someone other than the defendant has directly infringed the patent; (2) the defendant sold, offered for sale, or imported a component of the infringing product or an apparatus for use in the infringing process; (3) the component or apparatus is not a staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use; (4) the component or apparatus constitutes a material part of the patented invention; and (5) the defendant knew the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing product/method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use' is something with substantial non-infringing uses that are not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical. Contributory infringement requires an underlying direct infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal Infringement of Means-Plus-Function Claims (Proof Steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show literal infringement of a means-plus-function or step-plus-function claim element, plaintiff must prove that the accused structure/step that performs the claimed function is identical to or equivalent to the structure/step disclosed in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) decide whether accused product/method has any structure/step performing the recited function; (2) identify that structure/step in the accused product; (3) determine whether it is identical to or equivalent of the structure/step in the specification; if so, the means-plus-function requirement is satisfied for that element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Procedure Guidance for Jury
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury procedures: opening statements and closing arguments are not evidence; evidence is presented during witness testimony and exhibits; jurors should keep an open mind until all evidence is presented and should wait until deliberations phase to make decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain phases of trial (selection, opening, evidence, closing, instructions, deliberation). Depositions admitted at trial carry same weight as live testimony. Judge will instruct on law during the instructions phase and jurors must apply the law as instructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary Definitions to Guide Jury (Selected Terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide jurors with definitions of technical and legal terms used in the case (e.g., application, claims, prosecution history, ordinary skill in the art, prior art, specification, office action, license).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may prepare a glossary of technical terms to distribute; terms to be agreed by parties where appropriate.
